1	\section{Topology, localization and limits of variational arguments}
2	\label{S:nogo-topology}
3	
4	A useful approximation must be small in the topology in which the next
5	argument uses it. The obstructions below distinguish a local operator from a
6	Hilbert--Schmidt operator, a fixed spatial cutoff from a growing one, and
7	pointwise convergence from convergence of variational suprema. Throughout,
8	$a=\alpha_0\in(0,1)$ and $\Lambda=(1-\Delta)^{1/2}$, except that the positive
9	number $L$ denotes the temporal feature cutoff in No-go~\ref{P:nogo-32}.
10	
11	\subsection{The first driver cannot always be Hilbert--Schmidt}
12	\label{S:nogo-21}
13	
14	The one-dimensional operator construction suggests trying the same
15	Hilbert--Schmidt space in higher dimensions. A compact spatial observation
16	removes infinite volume, but it does not remove the following high-frequency
17	obstruction. The relevant compatibility is with the given noise, through its
18	bilinear first-driver tests.
19	
20	\setcounter{nogo}{20}
21	\begin{nogo}[A same-noise Hilbert--Schmidt obstruction]
22	  \label{P:nogo-21}
23	  Suppose that $d\in\{2,3\}$, $s\in\R$, and $0<T\le1$. Put
24	  $E_s=H^s(\R^d)\times H^{s-1}(\R^d)$ and let $S(t)$ be the massless wave
25	  phase group. For every nonzero covariance satisfying Hypothesis~\ref{H:homog},
26	  there are a nonnegative compact smooth physical coefficient mask $\zeta$ and
27	  a compact smooth observation cutoff $\chi$, equal to one on a sufficiently
28	  large ball, for which the localized Gaussian first-driver form has no
29	  compatible realization in $L^2(\Omega;\operatorname{HS}(E_s,E_s))$.
30	  Here compatibility means equality with the given $W$ for each fixed smooth
31	  phase pair, as specified in the proof.
32	\end{nogo}
33	
34	\begin{proof}
35	  First consider a deterministic coefficient $h(u,x)=k(u)H(x)$, where
36	  $H\in C_c^\infty(\R^d)$ is nonzero, even and nonnegative, and
37	  $k\in W^{1,\infty}[0,T]$ satisfies $k\ge k_0>0$. Write
38	  $B(b)(v,w)=(0,bv)$ and
39	  \[
40	    A_h=\int_0^T S(-u)B(h(u))S(u)\ud u,\qquad
41	    S(u,\xi)=\begin{pmatrix}
42	      \cos(u|\xi|)&\sin(u|\xi|)/|\xi|\\
43	      -|\xi|\sin(u|\xi|)&\cos(u|\xi|)
44	    \end{pmatrix}.
45	  \]
46	  The sine quotient has its continuous value at zero. The integral is a strong
47	  operator integral on $E_s$: $S(u)$ is strongly continuous and uniformly
48	  bounded on compact time intervals, and multiplication by $H$ is bounded on
49	  $H^s$. For the latter assertion, the weighted Fourier kernel is bounded in
50	  absolute value by a constant times
51	  $\langle\xi-\eta\rangle^{|s|}|\widehat H(\xi-\eta)|$, an integrable
52	  convolution kernel. This proves boundedness for every fixed real $s$.
53	
54	  Normalize the Fourier coordinates by
55	  $\operatorname{diag}(\langle\xi\rangle^s,\langle\xi\rangle^{s-1})$.
56	  Using the unitary Fourier transform, the lower-left block of $A_h$ then has
57	  kernel
58	  \[
59	    K_s(\xi,\eta)=(2\pi)^{-d/2}
60	    \langle\xi\rangle^{s-1}\langle\eta\rangle^{-s}
61	    \widehat H(\xi-\eta)
62	    \int_0^T k(u)\cos(u|\xi|)\cos(u|\eta|)\ud u.
63	  \]
64	  This formula follows from both phase coordinates: before applying the weights,
65	  the full product, with $r=|\xi|$, $\rho=|\eta|$, is
66	  \[
67	    \widehat H(\xi-\eta)
68	    \begin{pmatrix}
69	      -\dfrac{\sin(ru)}r\cos(\rho u)&
70	      -\dfrac{\sin(ru)}r\dfrac{\sin(\rho u)}\rho\\
71	      \cos(ru)\cos(\rho u)&\cos(ru)\dfrac{\sin(\rho u)}\rho
72	    \end{pmatrix}.
73	  \]
74	  All Fourier and time exchanges are justified on Schwartz pairs by the rapid
75	  decay of $\widehat H$ and then by density.
76	
77	  Let $J_0=\int_0^T k>0$ and
78	  $B_0=\|k\|_\infty+T\|k'\|_\infty$. Choose $\epsilon>0$ so that
79	  $\epsilon\le1$, $\epsilon T\le1$ and
80	  $\widehat H(z)\ge\widehat H(0)/2>0$ when $|z|\le\epsilon$.
81	  If $|\xi-\eta|\le\epsilon$, then
82	  \[
83	    \int_0^T k(u)\cos((r-\rho)u)\ud u\ge J_0/2,
84	    \qquad
85	    \left|\int_0^T k(u)\cos((r+\rho)u)\ud u\right|
86	    \le B_0/(r+\rho).
87	  \]
88	  The second bound is integration by parts in the absolutely continuous
89	  function $k$. Product-to-sum therefore bounds the time integral in $K_s$
90	  from below by $J_0/8$ when
91	  $r\ge R_0:=\max(1,2\epsilon,4B_0/J_0)$.
92	  On the same region,
93	  \[
94	    \langle\xi\rangle^{s-1}\langle\eta\rangle^{-s}
95	    =\langle\xi\rangle^{-1}
96	    (\langle\xi\rangle/\langle\eta\rangle)^s
97	    \ge 2^{-|s|}/(\sqrt2 r).
98	  \]
99	  Consequently, $|K_s(\xi,\eta)|\ge c_s/|\xi|$ there, for $c_s>0$.
100	  If $P_N$ cuts off Fourier frequencies to $B_N$, its truncated kernel is
101	  square integrable and Parseval followed by Tonelli gives
102	  \[
103	    \|P_NK_sP_N\|_{\operatorname{HS}}^2
104	    \ge c_s^2|B_\epsilon||\mathbb S^{d-1}|
105	    \int_{R_0}^{N-\epsilon}r^{d-3}\ud r\longrightarrow\infty.
106	  \]
107	  Indeed Parseval in the second kernel variable identifies its square integral
108	  with the sum of squared images of an orthonormal basis. If $A_h$ were
109	  Hilbert--Schmidt, every block compression would have bounded
110	  Hilbert--Schmidt norm. The displayed divergence proves otherwise. Real
111	  Hilbert--Schmidt operators and their complexifications have the same norm,
112	  so Fourier complexification has not changed the conclusion.
113	
114	  Suppose that $\operatorname{supp}H\subset B_A$, and let $\chi=1$ on
115	  $B_{A+T+1}$. With $D_\chi$ denoting multiplication of both phase coordinates,
116	  finite propagation gives
117	  \[
118	    D_\chi A_h=A_h=A_hD_\chi.
119	  \]
120	  For completeness, the local wave energy on a shrinking ball has boundary
121	  flux $v_t\partial_n v-(v_t^2+|\nabla v|^2)/2\le0$. Zero initial data
122	  therefore remain zero in the interior cone; time reversal gives the same
123	  support assertion for $S(-u)$. Apply this first to smooth data and then use
124	  Sobolev continuity and distributional testing to pass to $E_s$. The
125	  coefficient acts only in $B_A$, and the resulting output lies in
126	  $B_{A+T}$. Thus the failure persists after this compact observation.
127	
128	  We next produce $h$ as an actual covariance mean. Choose $L_0\ge1$ with
129	  $0<\Gamma(B_{L_0})<\infty$, and an even nonnegative $q\in C_c^\infty$
130	  equal to at least one on $B_{2L_0+1}$. Set $U=\Gamma*q$. Local finiteness
131	  of $\Gamma$ permits differentiation on every compact set, so $U$ is smooth,
132	  even and nonnegative, with $U(0)>0$. Moreover,
133	  \[
134	    Q=\int q(x)U(x)\ud x
135	    \ge |B_{L_0+1}|\Gamma(B_{L_0})>0.
136	  \]
137	  Choose an even nonnegative compact smooth $\zeta$, equal to one near zero,
138	  and put $H=\zeta U$. Choose $f\in C_c^\infty(0,1)$ nonnegative and
139	  nonzero, and set
140	  \[
141	    Z=W(f\otimes q),\qquad
142	    k(u)=\int_0^1|u-v|^{-a}f(v)\ud v.
143	  \]
144	  For $u\in[0,1]$, $k(u)\ge\int f>0$. Moving the derivative to the smooth
145	  zero extension of $f$ shows $k\in C^1[0,1]$, since $|\cdot|^{-a}$ is
146	  locally integrable. Also $\E Z^2=Q\int_0^1 f(u)k(u)\ud u\in(0,\infty)$.
147	  The mask is applied after the covariance convolution: $H=\zeta(\Gamma*q)$.
148	
149	  It remains to specify the compatible first-driver form with the correct
150	  Sobolev adjoint. For real Schwartz phases $z,w$ put
151	  \[
152	    v_u=[S(u)z]_1,\qquad
153	    G_w(u)=-\frac{\sin(u|D|)}{|D|}(\chi\Lambda^{2s}w_1)
154	    +\cos(u|D|)(\chi\Lambda^{2s-2}w_2),
155	  \]
156	  and define
157	  $F_{z,w}(u,x)=\mathbf1_{(0,T)}(u)\zeta(x)v_u(x)G_w(u,x)$.
158	  This test lies in the raw noise completion. In fact, on a fixed compact
159	  spatial support $K$, its covariance norm is bounded by a constant times
160	  $\|u\mapsto\|F(u)\|_\infty\|_{L^2(0,T)}$, by local Radon mass
161	  $\Gamma(K-K)$ and the time Schur bound for $|u-v|^{-a}$. Smooth interior
162	  time approximation gives membership. Define
163	  $\ell_\chi(z,w)=W(F_{z,w})$ on the given noise space.
164	  Direct transposition, with the Sobolev weights retained, gives
165	  \[
166	    G_w(u)=\Lambda^{2s-2}
167	    \big((D_\chi S(-u))^{*_{E_s}}w\big)_2.
168	  \]
169	  In particular, multiplication by $\chi$ has not been treated as self-adjoint
170	  in $E_s$. Absolute Fubini in the covariance pairing now gives
171	  \[
172	    \E[Z\ell_\chi(z,w)]
173	    =\int_0^T\!\int k(u)H(x)v_u(x)G_w(u,x)\ud x\ud u
174	    =\langle D_\chi A_hz,w\rangle_{E_s}
175	    =\langle A_hz,w\rangle_{E_s}.
176	  \]
177	  All spatial factors in the raw tests have compact support and the temporal
178	  singularity is integrable, which supplies the absolute Fubini bound.
179	
180	  If $X\in L^2(\Omega;\operatorname{HS}(E_s,E_s))$ satisfied
181	  $\langle Xz,w\rangle_{E_s}=\ell_\chi(z,w)$ almost surely for every fixed
182	  Schwartz pair, then Cauchy--Schwarz would make
183	  $Y=\E[ZX]$ a Hilbert--Schmidt Bochner integral. Continuous matrix evaluation
184	  would give $\langle Yz,w\rangle=\langle A_hz,w\rangle$ for all such pairs.
185	  Density implies $Y=A_h$, a contradiction. This proves No-go~\ref{P:nogo-21}.
186	\end{proof}
187	
188	This result concerns the same-index phase spaces $E_s$ and a compatible
189	$L^2$ Hilbert--Schmidt realization. It does not concern every cutoff: the zero
190	cutoff, for example, has no such obstruction. It is not a nonexistence result
191	for the Stratonovich solution or its moments. A route using loss of regularity
192	between input and output, operator norms, or a different Schatten class must
193	supply its own estimates; changing the fixed index $s$ alone cannot reopen
194	this particular route.

196	\subsection{A physical mask may not act on the noise quotient}
197	\label{S:nogo-22}
198	
199	A smooth physical mask is harmless on ordinary test functions. It need not
200	preserve the zero classes of a covariance seminorm. The following is the
201	obstruction already proved in Proposition~\ref{P:masked-quotient-obstruction};
202	we include its witness to explain why the auxiliary completion is needed.
203	
204	\setcounter{nogo}{21}
205	\begin{nogo}[A mask that separates noise-null representatives]
206	  \label{P:nogo-22}
207	  For $d=2$, $\alpha=1$, $0<a<1$ and
208	  $\Gamma=\delta_0(\ud x_1)\ud x_2$, there exist real compact smooth $F$ and
209	  a nonnegative smooth square mask $\zeta$ for which
210	  $\E W(F)^2=0$ but $\E W(\zeta F)^2>0$.
211	  Thus multiplication by this mask does not descend to the original noise
212	  quotient, and no finite uniform covariance-norm multiplier bound holds.
213	\end{nogo}
214	\begin{proof}
215	  Choose a nonnegative nonconstant compact smooth plateau function $\psi$ and
216	  put $\chi=\psi^2$. The spatial covariance seminorm is
217	  \[
218	    V(g)=\int_\R\left(\int_\R g(x_1,x_2)\ud x_2\right)^2\ud x_1.
219	  \]
220	  This also shows positive definiteness of the nonnegative even tempered
221	  measure $\Gamma$; its scaling is $\Gamma(cA)=c\Gamma(A)$, as required
222	  for $d=2$, $\alpha=1$. Put
223	  $g(x)=\chi(x_1)\chi''(x_2)$ and
224	  $\zeta(x)=\chi(x_1)\chi(x_2)=(\psi(x_1)\psi(x_2))^2$.
225	  Then $\int\chi''=0$, whereas integration by parts gives
226	  \[
227	    \int\zeta(x)g(x)\ud x_2=-\chi(x_1)^2\int(\chi')^2.
228	  \]
229	  Consequently, $V(g)=0$ and
230	  $V(\zeta g)=\int\chi^4\,\big(\int(\chi')^2\big)^2>0$.
231	  Tensor with a nonzero nonnegative $\tau\in C_c^\infty(0,T)$. Its temporal
232	  variance is finite and strictly positive, so $F=\tau\otimes g$ has the
233	  asserted full-noise variances. This proves No-go~\ref{P:nogo-22}.
234	\end{proof}
235	
236	This covariance is not two-dimensional spatial white noise. One can still
237	mask individual tests before taking an auxiliary completion. To reopen a
238	multiplier argument on the original quotient, one must first prove that the
239	chosen mask preserves its null space and then prove the required norm bound.

241	\subsection{Frequency decay does not give whole-space compactness}
242	\label{S:nogo-24}
243	
244	The compact-cutoff estimates use spatial confinement as well as frequency
245	smoothing. Removing the former loses compactness even for a deterministic
246	Bessel multiplier; see Proposition~\ref{P:cutoff-boundary-tests}.
247	
248	\setcounter{nogo}{23}
249	\begin{nogo}[Translations defeat whole-space compactness]
250	  \label{P:nogo-24}
251	  For every $d\ge1$ and $\gamma>0$, the operator $\Lambda^{-\gamma}$ on
252	  $L^2(\R^d)$ is not compact.
253	\end{nogo}
254	\begin{proof}
255	  Take a nonzero Schwartz function $f$ with Gaussian Fourier transform and put
256	  $g=\Lambda^{-\gamma}f$. Then $g$ is nonzero and Schwartz. For translations
257	  $T_hg(x)=g(x-h)$, Plancherel gives
258	  \[
259	    \langle T_hg,g\rangle
260	    =\int e^{-i\xi\cdot h}|\widehat g(\xi)|^2\ud\xi\longrightarrow0
261	    \quad (|h|\longrightarrow\infty).
262	  \]
263	  The limit follows, for example, by integration by parts in the Fourier
264	  transform of the Schwartz function $|\widehat g|^2$.
265	  Choose a sufficiently large spacing $b$ and $h_n=nb e_1$ so that distinct
266	  images $T_{h_n}g$ have squared distance at least $\|g\|_2^2$.
267	  The inputs $T_{h_n}f$ have constant norm and
268	  $\Lambda^{-\gamma}T_{h_n}f=T_{h_n}g$. Their images have no Cauchy
269	  subsequence. This proves No-go~\ref{P:nogo-24}.
270	\end{proof}
271	
272	Compact spatial cutoffs and the conditional Schatten estimates in the main
273	text survive. No necessity at a Schatten endpoint is asserted here. A
274	whole-space successor needs a tightness condition that prevents translation
275	of mass, or an explicitly different topology.

277	\subsection{Fixed projections do not control growing spatial masks}
278	\label{S:nogo-25}
279	
280	At each fixed radius the Cameron mean map can be compact. Its finite-rank
281	approximations need not be uniform in that radius. The following witness uses
282	actual unit controls for one-dimensional spatial white noise. The fixed-radius
283	map and its compact approximation are those of
284	Proposition~\ref{P:cameron-full-mean}.
285	
286	\setcounter{nogo}{24}
287	\begin{nogo}[Escape from every fixed smooth projection]
288	  \label{P:nogo-25}
289	  Let $\Gamma=\delta_0$ in $d=1$, and let $H_I$ be the closed raw-noise
290	  space generated by tests supported in $I\times\R$, $I=(0,1)$. Let $P_J$
291	  be any fixed finite-rank orthogonal projection in $H_I$ whose range is
292	  spanned by smooth compact tests supported in $I\times\R$. For the physical masked mean multiplier $T_R$ on
293	  $F=(H^{1/2}\times H^{-1/2})\oplus\R^2$, with the last coordinates
294	  representing constant displacement and velocity, one has, for every
295	  $2<r<2/a$,
296	  \[
297	    \sup_R\|T_R(I-P_J)\|_{H_I\to L^r((0,1);\mathcal K(F))}\ge c_a>0,
298	  \]
299	  where $c_a$ can be chosen independently of $J$. Here the smooth masks $m_R$
300	  equal one on $[-R,R]$. For a smooth control $\Psi$ with covariance mean
301	  $h_\Psi$, the operator sends $(v,w,c,d)$ to
302	  $(0,m_Rh_\Psi(s)(v+c),0,0)$.
303	\end{nogo}
304	\begin{proof}
305	  Use the temporal equilibrium density $f_a$ of
306	  Lemma~\ref{L:temporal-equilibrium}, so that
307	  $\int_0^1|s-t|^{-a}f_a(t)\ud t=1$ and
308	  $\|f_a\|_{H_a}^2=M_a>0$.
309	  Choose nonnegative $q\in C_c^\infty(\R)$ with $\|q\|_2=1$, and put
310	  $q_n(x)=q(x-x_n)$, where $x_n\to\infty$. The controls
311	  \[
312	    \Psi_n=\frac{f_a\otimes q_n}{\sqrt{M_a}}
313	  \]
314	  have unit raw norm and time-independent covariance mean
315	  $q_n/\sqrt{M_a}$. Membership follows by $L^2$ approximation of $f_a$ and
316	  the Schur bound for the temporal kernel.
317	  The finitely many tests spanning $P_J$ have common compact spatial support.
318	  For all sufficiently large $n$, spatial whiteness gives
319	  $P_J\Psi_n=0$ exactly. Choose $R_n$ to contain $\operatorname{supp}q_n$
320	  in the plateau of $m_{R_n}$.
321	
322	  The constant-displacement input $e=(0,0,1,0)$ has norm one. The phase dual
323	  \[
324	    w_n=(0,\Lambda q_n/\|q\|_{H^{1/2}},0,0)
325	  \]
326	  also has norm one. Indeed its velocity norm is $H^{-1/2}$, and translation
327	  preserves $\|q\|_{H^{1/2}}$. The mean multiplier sends $e$ to the velocity
328	  $q_n/\sqrt{M_a}$, so the $H^{-1/2}$ inner product gives, for every $s$,
329	  \[
330	    \langle T_{R_n}\Psi_n(s)e,w_n\rangle_F
331	    =\frac{\|q_n\|_2^2}{\sqrt{M_a}\|q\|_{H^{1/2}}}
332	    =:c_a>0.
333	  \]
334	  Integrating over the unit time interval proves the bound for all $r$ stated.
335	  This proves No-go~\ref{P:nogo-25}.
336	\end{proof}

340	For a fixed $R$, sufficiently distant translates miss its mask, so there is
341	no contradiction with fixed-radius compactness. A replacement must use
342	projections depending on the radius with quantitative control, or a different
343	localization argument. The witness does not exclude every such strategy.

345	\subsection{Two distinct limitations of block costs}
346	\label{S:nogo-26}
347	
348	A nonlinear block argument must handle both small perturbations and rare large
349	blocks. A power larger than one misses the first effect; an averaged budget
350	alone does not bound the largest block.
351	
352	\setcounter{nogo}{25}
353	\begin{nogo}[A pure Young power and a maximum from an average]
354	  \label{P:nogo-26}
355	  On $[0,1]$, with $\theta=2/3$ and $\nu=1/\theta=3/2$, no finite constant
356	  $C>0$ gives
357	  $\log U(1)\le C\|D\|_{C^\theta}^{\nu}$ for all scalar paths starting at zero
358	  and solving $\ud U=U\ud D$, $U(0)=1$, when
359	  $\|D\|_{C^\theta}=\|D\|_\infty+[D]_{C^\theta}$.
360	  Moreover, a bound on $N^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^N b_j^r$, $r>0$, does not give a
361	  bound independent of $N$ on $\max_j b_j$.
362	\end{nogo}
363	\begin{proof}
364	  For $D(t)=xt$, $x>0$, the solution is $U(t)=e^{xt}$ and
365	  $\|D\|_{C^{2/3}}=2x$. Taking $x=1/(16C^2)$ gives
366	  $C(2x)^{3/2}=x/\sqrt2<x=\log U(1)$.
367	  For the second assertion, take $b_1=N^{1/r}$ and $b_j=0$ for $j>1$.
368	  Their averaged $r$th power is one while their maximum tends to infinity.
369	  This proves No-go~\ref{P:nogo-26}.
370	\end{proof}
371	
372	A linear-plus-power cost is not refuted. For any $\tau>0$ and $\nu>1$,
373	$x\le\tau+\tau^{1-\nu}x^\nu$ gives an explicit alternative with slack.
374	Also, if $0<\nu<r$ and $N^{-1}\sum b_j^r\le M$, then H\"older gives
375	$N^{-1}\sum b_j^\nu\le M^{\nu/r}$, and
376	\[
377	  \frac1N\sum_{b_j>K}b_j^\nu\le K^{\nu-r}M.
378	\]
379	Thus an averaged tail argument survives. Reopening the block route requires
380	an actual evolution estimate with its linear term or slack, followed by an
381	averaged bad-block estimate. These scalar tests alone do not construct a
382	Cameron potential or prove a wave evolution bound.
383	
384	\subsection{Concentrating temporal controls restrict integrability}
385	\label{S:nogo-27}
386	
387	Compactness of a temporal mean map has a natural upper endpoint. A
388	concentrating control detects both excessive integrability and failure of
389	compactness at that endpoint.
390	
391	\setcounter{nogo}{26}
392	\begin{nogo}[The temporal concentration threshold]
393	  \label{P:nogo-27}
394	  Let $I=(0,1)$, $0<a<1$, and let $H_a$ be the completion of smooth tests for
395	  $\|f\|_{H_a}^2=\int_I\int_I f(t)f(s)|t-s|^{-a}\ud t\ud s$.
396	  On smooth tests set $C_af(t)=\int_I|t-s|^{-a}f(s)\ud s$.
397	  The map $C_a$ is not bounded from $H_a$ to $L^r(I)$ when $r>2/a$,
398	  including $r=\infty$, and it is not compact into $L^{2/a}(I)$.
399	\end{nogo}
400	\begin{proof}
401	  Choose $t_0\in I$ and a nonzero nonnegative
402	  $\phi\in C_c^\infty(-1,1)$. Put
403	  \[
404	    v_\phi=\int\!\int\phi(u)\phi(v)|u-v|^{-a}\ud u\ud v\in(0,\infty),
405	    \qquad
406	    f_\epsilon(t)=\frac{\epsilon^{a/2-1}}{\sqrt{v_\phi}}
407	    \phi((t-t_0)/\epsilon).
408	  \]
409	  For sufficiently small $\epsilon$, its support lies in $I$. Changing both
410	  variables shows $\|f_\epsilon\|_{H_a}=1$, and
411	  \[
412	    (C_af_\epsilon)(t_0+\epsilon y)
413	    =\frac{\epsilon^{-a/2}}{\sqrt{v_\phi}}
414	    \int|y-v|^{-a}\phi(v)\ud v.
415	  \]
416	  For $|y|\le1$, the last integral is at least $2^{-a}\int\phi>0$.
417	  Thus for finite $r$,
418	  $\|C_af_\epsilon\|_{L^r}\ge c_r\epsilon^{1/r-a/2}$, and the analogous
419	  supremum lower bound is $c\epsilon^{-a/2}$. This proves unboundedness above
420	  $2/a$.
421	  For every fixed $t\ne t_0$, on the other hand,
422	  $C_af_\epsilon(t)=O_t(\epsilon^{a/2})\to0$.
423	  At $r=2/a$ the norm lower bound stays strictly positive. If a subsequence
424	  converged strongly in this $L^r$ space, a further subsequence would converge
425	  almost everywhere to its strong limit. The limit would have to be zero,

4	The density in Lemma~\ref{L:temporal-equilibrium} is the classical interval
5	Riesz equilibrium density. Its probability-normalized form on $[-1,1]$ is
6	recalled by Calef and Hardin~\cite{calef.hardin:source2008:riesz}*{p.~1}.
7	We prove the potential identity with the normalization used here.
8	
9	We use Euler's function $\Gamma_E(x) = \int_0^\infty u^{x-1}e^{-u}\ud u$, $x >
10	0$, and $\operatorname{Beta}(x,y) = \int_0^1t^{x-1}(1-t)^{y-1}\ud t$, $x,y > 0$.
11	Both integrals are positive and finite.
12	
13	\begin{lemma}[Gamma and Beta identities]\label{L:equilibrium-gamma-beta}
14	  For positive arguments,
15	  \begin{align*}
16	    \Gamma_E(x+1)&=x\Gamma_E(x),\\
17	    \operatorname{Beta}(x,y)
18	    &=\frac{\Gamma_E(x)\Gamma_E(y)}{\Gamma_E(x+y)},\\
19	    \Gamma_E(2x)
20	    &=\frac{2^{2x-1}\Gamma_E(x)\Gamma_E(x+1/2)}{\sqrt\pi}.
21	  \end{align*}
22	\end{lemma}
23	
24	\begin{proof}
25	  Integration by parts gives the recurrence, with vanishing boundary terms. In
26	  the positive product Gamma integral, use $(u,v) = (Rt,R(1-t))$, with Jacobian
27	  $R$; Tonelli gives the Beta--Gamma identity. For the last identity, symmetry,
28	  then $t = (1+v)/2$ and $v^2 = w$, give $\operatorname{Beta}(x,x) =
29	  2^{1-2x}\operatorname{Beta}(1/2,x)$. Also $\Gamma_E(1/2) = \int_\R e^{-z^2}\ud
30	  z = \sqrt\pi$: the substitution $u = z^2$ gives the first equality, and
31	  squaring the positive Gaussian integral and using polar coordinates gives
32	  $2\pi\int_0^\infty re^{-r^2}\ud r = \pi$. Substituting these into the
33	  Beta--Gamma identity proves duplication. This proves
34	  Lemma~\ref{L:equilibrium-gamma-beta}.
35	\end{proof}

37	\begin{lemma}[Exact potential and mass]\label{L:temporal-equilibrium}
38	  For $0 < a < 1$ put $r = (1-a)/2$ and, for $0 < t < 1$,
39	  \begin{equation}\label{E:temporal-equilibrium-density}
40	    f_a(t)=\frac{[t(1-t)]^{-r}}{\Gamma_E(r)\Gamma_E(1-r)}.
41	  \end{equation}
42	  This positive function belongs to $L^1(0,1)\cap L^2(0,1)$, and
43	  \begin{align}
44	    \int_0^1|s-t|^{-a}f_a(t)\ud t&=1
45	    &&\text{for every }s\in[0,1],\label{E:temporal-equilibrium-potential}\\
46	    M_a:=\int_0^1f_a(t)\ud t
47	    &=\frac{\Gamma_E((1+a)/2)}
48	    {\Gamma_E(1+a)\Gamma_E((1-a)/2)}>0.
49	    \label{E:temporal-equilibrium-mass}
50	  \end{align}
51	\end{lemma}

53	\begin{proof}
54	  The positive binomial series $(1-z)^{-p} = \sum_{n\ge0}(p)_nz^n/n!$, $p > 0$,
55	  $0 \le z < 1$, follows directly as follows. Its coefficient ratio gives
56	  uniform convergence on compact subintervals, including for its derivative.
57	  Termwise differentiation gives $(1-z)y' = py$, $y(0) = 1$; hence $(1-z)^py$ is
58	  constant one. Here $(p)_0 = 1$, $(p)_n = p(p+1)\cdots(p+n-1)$. All terms used
59	  below are nonnegative, so Tonelli applies.

61	  For $0 < s < 1$ split the integral of $|s-t|^{2r-1}[t(1-t)]^{-r}$ into left
62	  and right parts. In the left part, $t = su$ gives

64	    L(s)
65	    &=s^r\int_0^1(1-u)^{2r-1}u^{-r}(1-su)^{-r}\ud u\\
66	    &=\operatorname{Beta}(1-r,2r)s^r
67	    \sum_{n\ge0}
68	    \frac{(r)_n(1-r)_ns^n}{(1+r)_n n!}.
69	  \end{align*}
70	  The Beta ratio follows from the Gamma recurrence. Since $(r)_n/(1+r)_n =
71	  r/(r+n)$, expanding the incomplete Beta integral gives
72	  \[
73	    L(s)=r\operatorname{Beta}(1-r,2r)B_s(r,r),\qquad
74	    B_s(r,r)=\int_0^s u^{r-1}(1-u)^{r-1}\ud u.
75	  \]

77	  $B_s(r,r)+B_{1-s}(r,r) = \operatorname{Beta}(r,r)$. The full integral is
78	  therefore $r\operatorname{Beta}(1-r,2r)\operatorname{Beta}(r,r) =
